title: Future Plans
subtitle: Say what you are going to do and what you will do

lessons.title: Je vais partir
lessons.description: Use the futur proche (aller + infinitive) to talk about what is about to happen.

blocks.heading: aller + infinitive = going to
blocks.body: To talk about the near future, French uses the verb "aller" (to go) followed by another verb in the infinitive. It works exactly like English "I am going to leave". You only conjugate "aller" — the second verb never changes.

examples.french: Je vais partir demain.
examples.english: I am going to leave tomorrow.

examples.french: Tu vas prendre le train ?
examples.english: Are you going to take the train?

examples.french: Elle va réserver un hôtel.
examples.english: She is going to book a hotel.

examples.french: Nous allons faire nos valises ce soir.
examples.english: We are going to pack our bags tonight.

examples.french: Ils vont arriver tout à l'heure.
examples.english: They are going to arrive in a little while.

blocks.tip: The futur proche is by far the most common future in spoken French. If you only learn one future form, learn this one.

blocks.heading: Words that announce the near future
blocks.body: Certain time expressions almost always go with the futur proche: bientôt, tout de suite, ce soir, demain, la semaine prochaine. They usually sit at the beginning or the end of the sentence.

examples.french: Je vais bientôt déménager.
examples.english: I am going to move house soon.

examples.french: On va manger tout de suite.
examples.english: We are going to eat right away.

examples.french: Ce soir, je vais préparer mon sac à dos.
examples.english: Tonight, I am going to pack my backpack.

examples.french: La semaine prochaine, ils vont visiter Paris.
examples.english: Next week, they are going to visit Paris.

examples.french: Nous allons partir dans une heure.
examples.english: We are going to leave in an hour.

blocks.heading: Saying what you are NOT going to do
blocks.body: In the negative, "ne … pas" wraps around the conjugated verb "aller", not around the infinitive. Object pronouns go directly in front of the infinitive.

examples.french: Je ne vais pas rester à l'hôtel.
examples.english: I am not going to stay at the hotel.

examples.french: Elle ne va pas rentrer avant minuit.
examples.english: She is not going to get home before midnight.

examples.french: On ne va jamais oublier ce voyage.
examples.english: We are never going to forget this trip.

examples.french: Je vais te retrouver à la gare.
examples.english: I am going to meet you at the station.

examples.french: Il va nous accompagner à l'aéroport.
examples.english: He is going to go with us to the airport.

blocks.tip: "On va…" is the everyday way to say "we are going to…" — much more common in speech than "nous allons…".

blocks.heading: Conjugating "aller" in the present
blocks.body: The futur proche only works if "aller" is correct: je vais, tu vas, il/elle/on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. Everything after it stays in the infinitive — no ending changes, no agreement.

examples.french: Je vais réserver le billet.
examples.english: I am going to book the ticket.

examples.french: Tu vas voyager seul ?
examples.english: Are you going to travel alone?

examples.french: On va prendre le TGV.
examples.english: We are going to take the high-speed train.

examples.french: Vous allez rester combien de jours ?
examples.english: How many days are you going to stay?

examples.french: Elles vont dormir chez une amie.
examples.english: They are going to sleep at a friend's place.

blocks.tip: Never write "je vais je pars". After "aller" the verb has no subject and no ending: "je vais partir".

blocks.heading: Reflexive and pronoun verbs in the futur proche
blocks.body: With reflexive verbs, the reflexive pronoun matches the subject and sits just before the infinitive: je vais me lever, tu vas te lever, nous allons nous lever. Other object pronouns work the same way.

examples.french: Je vais me lever à cinq heures.
examples.english: I am going to get up at five.

examples.french: Tu vas te reposer dans le train.
examples.english: You are going to rest on the train.

examples.french: Nous allons nous retrouver au quai 3.
examples.english: We are going to meet on platform 3.

examples.english: He is going to hurry.

examples.french: Je ne vais pas me coucher tard.
examples.english: I am not going to go to bed late.

lessons.title: Demain, je ferai...
lessons.description: Build the futur simple, including the irregular stems you meet every day.

blocks.heading: The futur simple: infinitive + endings
blocks.body: For most verbs the futur simple is built on the whole infinitive plus one set of endings: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. With -re verbs, drop the final -e first (prendre → prendr-). The endings never change, whatever the verb.

examples.french: Demain, je parlerai avec le directeur.
examples.english: Tomorrow, I will speak with the director.

examples.french: Tu finiras ton stage en juin.
examples.english: You will finish your internship in June.

examples.french: Elle prendra le train de dix heures.
examples.english: She will take the ten o'clock train.

examples.french: Nous habiterons près de la mer.
examples.english: We will live near the sea.

examples.french: Ils arriveront la semaine prochaine.
examples.english: They will arrive next week.

blocks.tip: The endings are the present tense of "avoir" (ai, as, a, [av]ons, [av]ez, ont) glued to the infinitive — an easy way to remember them.

blocks.heading: The irregular stems you really need
blocks.body: About fifteen very common verbs use a special stem, but they still take the same endings. Learn these as a block: être → ser-, avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, venir → viendr-, pouvoir → pourr-, vouloir → voudr-, devoir → devr-, savoir → saur-, voir → verr-.

examples.french: Je serai à Paris jeudi.
examples.english: I will be in Paris on Thursday.

examples.french: Nous aurons plus de temps en août.
examples.english: We will have more time in August.

examples.french: Il ira à l'université l'année prochaine.
examples.english: He will go to university next year.

examples.french: Qu'est-ce que tu feras après le bac ?

examples.french: Vous pourrez me téléphoner ce soir.
examples.english: You will be able to call me tonight.

examples.french: Elles viendront avec leurs enfants.
examples.english: They will come with their children.

blocks.heading: Futur proche or futur simple?
blocks.body: The futur proche feels close, concrete and personal; the futur simple feels further away, more planned or more formal. In writing, forecasts and official plans, the futur simple is the normal choice.

examples.french: Je vais téléphoner tout de suite.
examples.english: I am going to call right away.

examples.french: Je téléphonerai la semaine prochaine.

examples.french: Un jour, nous achèterons une maison.

blocks.tip: Nobody will misunderstand you if you pick the "wrong" one — but sounding natural means using the futur proche for everyday spoken plans.

blocks.heading: The full set of futur simple endings
blocks.body: Take "parler": je parlerai, tu parleras, il/elle parlera, nous parlerons, vous parlerez, ils/elles parleront. Notice that every form keeps the -r sound of the infinitive — that -r is the signal that a French verb is in the future.

examples.french: Je finirai ce travail avant midi.
examples.english: I will finish this work before noon.

examples.french: Tu choisiras ton université en mai.
examples.english: You will choose your university in May.

examples.french: Nous vendrons la voiture cet été.
examples.english: We will sell the car this summer.

examples.french: Vous attendrez cinq minutes.
examples.english: You will wait five minutes.

examples.french: Ils répondront demain matin.
examples.english: They will answer tomorrow morning.

blocks.tip: If you can hear a clear "r" before the ending, you are hearing a future: "je parlerai" (future) vs "je parlais" (imperfect).

blocks.heading: quand / dès que + futur
blocks.body: After "quand", "dès que" and "lorsque", French uses the future where English uses the present. English says "when I arrive, I will call you"; French says "quand j'arriverai, je t'appellerai" — both verbs in the future.

lessons.title: Mes projets
lessons.description: Talk about goals and hopes with espérer, avoir l'intention de, and si + présent + futur.

blocks.heading: espérer + verb: saying what you hope
blocks.body: "Espérer" means "to hope". Followed directly by an infinitive it means you hope to do something yourself: j'espère voyager. Followed by "que" plus a new subject, French keeps the indicative — usually the present or the future.

examples.french: J'espère trouver un travail cet été.
examples.english: I hope to find a job this summer.

examples.french: Nous espérons déménager en juin.
examples.english: We hope to move in June.

examples.french: J'espère que tu viendras.
examples.english: I hope you will come.

examples.french: Elle espère que ses parents seront d'accord.
examples.english: She hopes her parents will agree.

examples.french: J'espère que tout ira bien.
examples.english: I hope everything will go well.

blocks.tip: Careful with the accents: j'espère, tu espères, il espère — but nous espérons, vous espérez. The accent flips with the stress.

blocks.heading: avoir l'intention de / compter / prévoir de
blocks.body: To announce a firm plan, French has three very useful structures, all followed by an infinitive: avoir l'intention de (to intend to), avoir l'idée de and prévoir de (to plan to). They are stronger and more deliberate than a simple futur proche.

examples.french: J'ai l'intention de reprendre mes études.
examples.english: I intend to go back to studying.

examples.french: Ils ont l'intention d'ouvrir un restaurant.
examples.english: They intend to open a restaurant.

examples.french: Nous prévoyons de partir en septembre.
examples.english: We are planning to leave in September.

examples.french: Elle a l'intention de passer son permis.
examples.english: She intends to take her driving test.

examples.french: Je n'ai pas l'intention d'abandonner.
examples.english: I have no intention of giving up.

blocks.tip: Watch the elision: "de" becomes "d'" before a vowel — avoir l'intention d'apprendre, d'ouvrir, d'étudier.

blocks.heading: si + présent, + futur
blocks.body: To say what will happen under a condition, French uses "si" plus the PRESENT tense, and the futur simple in the other half of the sentence. Never put a future after "si" itself — that is the single most common mistake at this level.

examples.french: Si j'ai assez d'argent, je voyagerai en Asie.
examples.english: If I have enough money, I will travel to Asia.

examples.french: Si tu travailles bien, tu réussiras.
examples.english: If you work well, you will succeed.

examples.french: S'il fait beau, nous irons à la mer.
examples.english: If the weather is nice, we will go to the seaside.

examples.french: Si elle obtient le stage, elle déménagera à Nantes.
examples.english: If she gets the internship, she will move to Nantes.

examples.french: Je t'aiderai si tu me le demandes.
examples.english: I will help you if you ask me to.

blocks.tip: "Si" shortens to "s'" only before il and ils: s'il, s'ils — but never before elle: si elle.

blocks.heading: The si-sentence in both directions
blocks.body: The two halves of a si-sentence can swap places. "Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai" and "Je viendrai si j'ai le temps" mean exactly the same thing. When "si" starts the sentence, a comma separates the two halves; when it comes second, there is no comma.

examples.english: I will come if I have time.

blocks.tip: Test yourself: if you have written "si + futur", something is wrong. "Si je serai" does not exist; say "si je suis".

blocks.heading: Verbs of hoping and intending: which form follows?
blocks.body: espérer + infinitive (same subject) or espérer que + indicative (new subject). avoir l'intention de / prévoir de / envisager de / rêver de are all followed by the infinitive. Only "compter" takes a bare infinitive with no preposition.

examples.english: I hope to leave in May.

examples.english: I hope you will leave in May.

passages.title: Les projets de Sofia
passages.french:
Sofia a vingt-trois ans et elle habite encore chez ses parents, à Toulouse.
Elle a l'intention de changer complètement de vie cette année.
Son rêve, c'est de travailler dans le tourisme et de voir d'autres pays.
Elle espère d'abord obtenir un stage dans une agence de voyages.
Si elle réussit son entretien la semaine prochaine, elle commencera en septembre.
Elle épargne aussi un peu d'argent chaque mois pour passer son permis de conduire.
« Si j'ai mon permis, je pourrai travailler partout dans la région », explique-t-elle.
Ses parents sont un peu inquiets, mais ils l'aideront quand même.
Sofia n'abandonnera pas : elle sait que la réussite demande du temps et des efforts.
passages.english:
Sofia is twenty-three and she still lives at her parents' place, in Toulouse.
She intends to change her life completely this year.
Her dream is to work in tourism and to see other countries.
She hopes first to get an internship at a travel agency.
If she does well in her interview next week, she will start in September.
She is also saving a little money each month to take her driving test.
"If I have my licence, I will be able to work anywhere in the region," she explains.
Her parents are a little worried, but they will help her anyway.
Sofia will not give up: she knows that success takes time and effort.
